91122390.title: 2011_Sawyerville–Eoline_tornado
91122390.extract:
# 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline Tornado

On April 27, 2011, a destructive low-end EF3 tornado moved across central Alabama, tracking across Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties along a path spanning 72.1 miles (116.0 km). The tornado affected areas near several towns, including Tishabee, Sawyerville, Havana, and Eoline. The tornado killed seven people and injured 52 others, while causing damage to hundreds of structures across its track. It occurred as part of the 2011 Super Outbreak, the largest tornado outbreak in recorded history, and was one of 22 EF3-rated tornadoes confirmed during that event.

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado initially formed in Greene County with EF1 intensity before escalating to EF2 strength and ultimately reaching peak EF3 intensity with maximum wind speeds of 145 miles per hour (233 km/h). The tornado maintained considerable destructive power as it traversed multiple counties, particularly affecting the areas around Sawyerville and Eoline where it produced severe structural damage. The tornado gradually weakened before lifting east of West Blocton.

# Meteorological Synopsis

The environmental conditions preceding the 2011 Super Outbreak were exceptionally conducive to violent tornado development. On April 25, 2011, a vigorous upper-level shortwave trough moved into the Southern Plains states, combining with ample instability, low-level moisture, and strong wind shear to fuel significant tornado development. The initial severe weather outbreak on April 25 produced at least 64 tornadoes across Texas and the surrounding region. On April 26, an additional approximately 50 tornadoes touched down as a consolidated area of low pressure traveled eastward across the region.

The most destructive period of the outbreak occurred on April 27, 2011, when atmospheric conditions reached extreme levels of instability and wind shear. The Storm Prediction Center issued a moderate risk of severe weather across the region in the days leading up to the outbreak and ultimately issued a high risk outlook on the morning of April 27 for a large portion of the affected area. Upper-air soundings taken at 1800 UTC on April 27 showed moderate to high instability due to steep lapse rates and strong wind shear indicated by significant hodographs. This extreme atmospheric setup resulted in 224 tornadoes touching down on April 27 alone from midnight to midnight CDT, breaking the previous single-day tornado record set during the 1974 Super Outbreak.

# Tornado Track and Damage

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado touched down in far southwest Greene County near the Tombigbee River just west of Tishabee on County Road 69, beginning with EF1-intensity damage. As the tornado moved northeast across rural Greene County north of Forkland, it destroyed at least 4 mobile homes, 3 outbuildings, and 2 churches, along with numerous trees. Two minor injuries were reported in Greene County during this initial phase.

The tornado intensified as it crossed the Black Warrior River and entered Hale County west of Sawyerville. Upon crossing Alabama Route 14 just north of Sawyerville, the tornado strengthened to EF3 intensity with estimated winds of 145 mph. Extensive structural damage was documented in the areas crossed by the tornado in Hale County as it progressed northeast through County Road 18, County Road 21, Alabama Highway 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram. At least 40 injuries and 6 fatalities occurred in Hale County. Numerous mobile homes and single-family homes were damaged or destroyed, along with one church, while thousands of trees were knocked down along the path.

The tornado continued into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, where it caused significant tree damage extending to the Bibb County line. The tornado then moved through Eoline, producing damage consistent with EF3 intensity and winds of 145 mph. In Eoline, numerous mobile homes and single-family homes sustained minor to major damage, with approximately a dozen structures destroyed. Notably, the Eoline Fire Department building and one business were destroyed. One fatality occurred in a vehicle near the fire department. An additional 10 injuries were recorded in Eoline.

Following its passage through Eoline, the tornado crossed Alabama Highway 5 south of West Blocton, where it weakened to EF2 intensity with winds of approximately 125 mph. Several mobile homes and single-family homes sustained major damage or were destroyed near County Road 26, with thousands of trees downed along the path. The tornado continued to weaken as it progressed northeast, ultimately lifting just northeast of Marvel.

Tornado warnings were in effect for Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties from 4:50 p.m. until 7:45 p.m. CDT.

# Context Within the 2011 Super Outbreak

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was one component of a historic and unprecedented tornado outbreak that affected the Southern, Midwestern, and Northeastern United States from April 25 to 28, 2011. The 2011 Super Outbreak produced a total of 368 confirmed tornadoes across 21 states, making it the largest tornado outbreak on record. In Alabama alone, 62 confirmed tornadoes occurred on April 27, with 238 tornado-related deaths recorded in the state during the entire outbreak.

The outbreak produced 22 EF3-rated tornadoes, 11 EF4-rated tornadoes, and 4 EF5-rated tornadoes during the four-day period. Among the most destructive tornadoes of the outbreak were the Hackleburg–Phil Campbell EF5 tornado and the Tuscaloosa–Birmingham EF4 tornado, both of which produced catastrophic damage and significant loss of life in Alabama. The total damage from the 2011 Super Outbreak exceeded $10 billion (2011 USD), making it the costliest tornado outbreak in United States history.
